chunks: From him, from al-Qasim and Fadalah, from al-Kahili, who said:

A man asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) while I was with him about a group of Muslims who were visited by a Magian man: Should they invite him to their food? He said, 'As for me, I do not invite him, nor do I let him join us (eat with us), for I dislike that I should prohibit upon you something that you do in your lands.'

key_terms.أُوَاكِلُهُ: I let him join us / I eat with him

ai.seo_question: Should Muslims invite non-Muslims to eat with them according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) distinguishes between personal strictness and general legal flexibility (*rukhas*), explaining that his refusal to eat with or delegate to a Magian is a precautionary measure to avoid becoming a binding precedent for the community. This reflects the Shia scholarly principle that the practices of the Imams, while authoritative, may be tailored to specific contexts to prevent imposing undue hardship (*haraj*) on the general populace in diverse geographical settings.
